India's sharp fall in extreme poverty as global progress slows

India has sharply reduced extreme poverty, but the global fight is losing momentum. Explore what three poverty lines reveal about India's states, its neighbours and the wider world.

01 · India

Same survey, same year, three answers

The World Bank uses three daily poverty lines per person: $3 measures extreme poverty; $4.20 and $8.30 reflect poverty standards in lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income countries.

The amounts are adjusted for what money can buy in different countries. Switch the line to see how India’s 2023–24 survey tells three different stories.

    03 · Who remains

    Who is still below the line

    At the $4.20 line, about 22 in every 100 children live in poor households, compared with about 14 in every 100 working-age adults. Poverty is also more common in rural areas and among people with little schooling.

    The billions between the two lines

    About 2.9 billion people, or 36 in every 100 worldwide, lived above $3 but below $8.30 a day in 2024. Escaping extreme poverty is not the same as reaching financial security.

    For 2026, the World Bank projects 811 million people below $3 and about 3.7 billion below $8.30.

    Why is global progress slowing?

    Rapid growth in Asia drove much of the earlier fall. With extreme poverty now low in many of those economies, further gains depend increasingly on countries held back by weak growth, too few productive jobs, conflict and fragility.

    The World Bank’s October 2026 report says nine economies account for more than half of the world’s extremely poor. By 2030, it projects that 87% will live in Sub-Saharan Africa, in fragile or conflict-affected countries, or both.

    A separate May 2026 World Bank analysis found that, over the preceding decade, extreme poverty rose in Nigeria, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Pakistan and Sudan. It fell modestly in DR Congo and Tanzania, and sharply in India.

    10 · The bigger picture

    Poverty has fallen. Prosperity is another question.

    India has made major progress against extreme poverty. But the higher poverty lines show how far living standards still have to rise.

    The World Bank says further progress will increasingly depend on creating productive employment in the states where poverty remains concentrated.

    How we checked the data

    Methodology and source notes

    Which figures are comparable?

    The $3, $4.20 and $8.30 lines measure daily per-person consumption or income in 2021 purchasing-power-parity (PPP) dollars, not US dollars exchanged at today's rate. We do not print rupee equivalents, because converting the thresholds for a particular Indian survey year requires a survey-specific price deflator. These World Bank lines are not India's official national poverty line.

    Which source and year do the global charts use?

    The 2024 world pictogram and regional ranking come from the World Bank September 2026 PIP Technical Note 53 (Tables 1–2): 10.1% (824.3 million) at $3, 18.2% (1,482.8 million) at $4.20 and 46.2% (3,758.1 million) at $8.30. The 2.9 billion figure between the $3 and $8.30 thresholds is the 2024 difference: 3,758.1 million minus 824.3 million = 2,933.8 million. The 2026 estimates of 811 million at $3 and 3.7 billion at $8.30 are modelled nowcasts published in the October flagship report, not 2024 survey observations. The historical chart uses 43.4% in 1990 and 11.1% in 2018 from WDI table 1.2.2, and 9.8% in 2026 from Technical Note 53, Table 1. The 1950 figure is a historical reconstruction. WDI currently leaves the 2019 world rate blank; we do not fill that gap with an unsupported value.

    Why are Pakistan and Afghanistan outside the South Asia row?

    The regional rates are the World Bank’s harmonised estimates for reference year 2024, published in its September 2026 PIP update. They use the Bank’s current statistical grouping: Pakistan and Afghanistan moved from South Asia to the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region effective 1 July 2025. This is a change in the Bank’s statistical classification, not a change to geographical definitions. The neighbours chapter remains a separate editorial comparison.

    Which sources explain the global slowdown?

    The October 26, 2026 report and its announcement supply the nine-economy concentration finding and the 2030 projection of 87% in Sub-Saharan Africa, fragile and conflict-affected situations, or both. The latter is a union of overlapping categories, not two shares to add. The separate May 2026 Atlas analysis describes an eight-country comparison over its preceding decade; it is not a list of the October report’s nine economies. Its countries are examples of differing trajectories, not an attribution of the entire global slowdown. The long-run chart retains its audited 2018 benchmark and does not insert a numerical 2019 observation.

    Why do country comparisons use different years?

    The explorer uses the October 2026 briefs’ Poverty at Different Lines tables, rather than common-year estimates. Some narratives discuss newer results than those tables; for example, Brazil’s card uses the 2024 table and its trend card uses the narrative’s 2025 result. For India the source year is 2023 (2023–24 HCES); for Pakistan 2024 (2024–25); and for Sri Lanka 2019, before its economic crisis. Sri Lanka's brief projects worsening poverty after that survey. Pakistan's official national poverty measure (22% in 2018–19 to 29% in 2024–25) is separate from the international thresholds. All country dots are equally weighted: the explorer is not a population-weighted world average. Of 118 briefs, 112 have a $3 value, 112 a $4.20 value and 116 an $8.30 value. Missing entries are omitted, not zero.

    China, rounding and annual changes

    China's October 2026 brief contradicts itself for the 2022 $8.30 estimate: its narrative states 21.3%, while its detailed Poverty and Inequality Indicators table shows 21.5% (304.0 million people). The World Bank's WDI indicator and ESG data portal corroborate 21.3% for 2022, so we use 21.3% consistently in the explorer and India–China graphic. The table's 21.5% remains a publishing inconsistency. The World Bank also estimates 15.2% for 2024 using a modelled update; the explorer instead uses the 2022 survey-based rate, consistently with the October country briefs. The displayed China $3 rate of 0.0% is rounded, not a claim that nobody is poor. India's substantial 2022–23 to 2023–24 decline partly reflects improved survey implementation and reporting, according to the World Bank; therefore the story emphasizes the long-term 2011–12 to 2023–24 comparison.

    How do survey methods affect India’s comparison?

    The 2011–12 CES and 2022–23 and 2023–24 HCES are broadly comparable, but survey methods have improved. The World Bank says the most recent one-year fall reflects better measurement as well as gains in living standards. The estimated 49.6 crore reduction at $4.20 is its long-term 2011–12 to 2023–24 comparison, not a count independently reconstructed by TOI.

    How should the demographic comparisons be read?

    The rates are shares of each demographic group below $4.20 a day in the 2023–24 survey. Schooling comparisons cover ages 16 and above. They use household consumption per person; they do not show who controls money or how resources are shared within a home. The comparisons describe patterns, not the causes of poverty.

    How were the jobs scenarios calculated?

    The two global scenarios come from the World Bank’s October 26, 2026 report announcement. One asks what happens if employment among working-age adults in poor households reaches 75%; the other asks what happens if poor workers’ education reaches the average of people above the extreme-poverty line. The Bank models roughly one-fifth less extreme poverty in the first case, and nearly half less in the second, with predicted earnings up around 40%. These are hypothetical worldwide results, not causal evaluations, policy forecasts or separate reductions to be summed.

    What other measures are different?

    The US official poverty measure, the EU risk of poverty or social exclusion, and the UNDP multidimensional poverty index use different definitions and populations. Their totals cannot be combined with international-dollar poverty counts. The country trend cards link reported endpoints, not a continuously observed annual series. Coverage varies: Argentina’s survey is urban; Ethiopia, Honduras, Lebanon, Myanmar, Nigeria, South Sudan and Ukraine omit specified areas, as noted on their cards. The geographical exclusions follow Technical Note 53, PDF page 11, Table 6; Argentina is discussed on PDF page 10 and Ethiopia in its brief. Country-specific comparability breaks also affect interpretation. Published figures may be revised in future PIP releases.

    India's state-level rates, estimated numbers and the 57% finding

    Rates: World Bank Subnational Poverty and Inequality Database (SPID), AM26 / September 2026 release. In AM26 - SPID data.xlsx, filter the Data sheet for code=IND, year=2023, data=ALL and data_group=ALL. The 36 state/UT observations are in rows 48827–48862. Columns R, S and T hold the respective $3, $4.20 and $8.30 poverty headcount proportions in 2021 PPP; the display multiplies these by 100. The previous-year comparison is at rows 48575–48610. These are monetary-consumption measures, not NITI Aayog's multidimensional poverty indicator.

    Estimated numbers: TOI calculation, not a published World Bank state count. We multiply each 2023–24 state poverty rate by that jurisdiction's 1 March 2023 projected population (rural plus urban) from the Indian Health Ministry workbook Population_Projections_Health_Ministry.xlsx, stata_sheet, supplied inside the World Bank's India reproducibility package. We combine Dadra and Nagar Haveli with Daman and Diu to match SPID. The sum of all 36 state/UT estimates is the denominator for the displayed state share of the estimated national poor population. The projections sum to 1,388,166,000 people, matching the sum-based India row in the workbook’s stata_sheet. This is 3,000 above the original Ministry Table 8 national projection of 1,388,163,000 (MoH_pop_projections_orginial, B20), a 0.00022% difference consistent with adding jurisdiction figures rounded to thousands; we retain those inputs without rescaling. Summing the rounded state counts gives 35,970,002 people below $3, 225,239,118 below $4.20 and 1,111,847,284 below $8.30. At full precision, the corresponding weighted rates are 2.591%, 16.226% and 80.095%, compared with the brief’s 2.6%, 16.1% and 80.0%. The Ministry’s population base differs from WDI, which reports 1,438,069,596 for India in 2023; these reconstructed counts are not official national World Bank totals. Each state share divides its rounded count by the sum of all 36 rounded counts. Counts and shares are approximations, not survey microdata-derived counts. One-year changes should not be treated as durable trends.

    57% belt: World Bank October 2026 India Poverty & Equity Brief, PDF page 1, says about 57% of India's poor live in a contiguous belt stretching from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal. It does not provide the exact member states or explicitly specify the threshold used for that percentage. No arbitrary collection of states is shown as the World Bank's official 57% belt. Displayed counts and poverty rates can therefore inform the geography, but are not represented as a proof or official disaggregation of the 57% finding.

    Map: State and UT shapes were recovered from an earlier SmartViz SVG documenting Survey of India ABDB 1:1 million geometry; the underlying path coordinates were preserved. Source attribution does not constitute government endorsement. The applicable Survey of India reproduction permission and final TOI map-desk cartographic clearance must be obtained before publication. Displayed 0.0% values can be rounded rates; they do not prove no poor people exist.
